title: Refugee and migrant health is being reframed as core public-health, migration-governance, development, and universal-coverage infrastructure rather than a parallel humanitarian service
source_unit: WHO, World report on promoting the health of refugees and migrants: Monitoring progress on the WHO global action plan
geography: Global; all six WHO regions and countries implementing the 2019-2030 Global Action Plan on Promoting the Health of Refugees and Migrants

observations.period: 2026 report; first global baseline for the 2019-2030 WHO Global Action Plan

denominator.unit: WHO Member States completing the first Global Survey on Health and Migration in early 2025

baseline.value: The report provides the first global baseline for assessing implementation of the WHO Global Action Plan on Promoting the Health of Refugees and Migrants

integration_scope.value: Refugee and migrant health is assessed within public health, migration governance, development, and universal health coverage agendas

regional_coverage.unit: WHO regions represented by global evidence, policy analysis, and country case studies

observations.method: WHO global report structured around six Global Action Plan priority areas, combining the 93-country Global Survey on Health and Migration, global evidence, policy analysis, and country case studies from all six WHO regions.
observations.uncertainty: A country-reported implementation survey is not a complete measure of service quality, access, health outcomes, or lived experience; participation and reporting capacity may vary across countries and policy domains.
observations.subgroup: Refugees, asylum-seekers, migrants in different legal and work statuses, host communities, health systems, migration authorities, and public-health and development institutions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Embedding migrant health in national systems can improve continuity and equity, but formal integration may coexist with exclusionary eligibility rules, detention, fear of authorities, language barriers, or uneven implementation.

observations.period: 2026 report; six priority areas of the WHO Global Action Plan

denominator.unit: Global Action Plan priority areas used to structure the report

priority_structure.value: The report consolidates implementation evidence across the six priority areas of the Global Action Plan

cross_sector_route.value: The implementation route joins health equity and system resilience to migration governance, development, universal health coverage, leadership, investment, coordination, data, and participation

recommended_roadmaps.value: WHO recommends national implementation roadmaps, stronger monitoring systems, cross-sector partnerships, and inclusion of refugees and migrants in decision-making

observations.method: WHO synthesis of the Global Action Plan's six priority areas, survey findings, policy analysis, and country examples.
observations.uncertainty: The public summary does not enumerate the country-level performance of each priority area or establish which recommendations are most effective under different legal, fiscal, conflict, or health-system conditions.
observations.subgroup: National ministries, health providers, local authorities, migrant and refugee organizations, civil society, employers, schools, and people on the move.
observations.counterinterpretation: Roadmaps and coordination mechanisms can become administrative overlays without budget, workforce, legal protection, interpretation, data safeguards, and accountability to affected people.

observations.period: 2026; health equity and system resilience for people on the move

health_equity.value: The report frames migrant- and refugee-inclusive action as essential to health equity

system_resilience.value: The report links inclusive refugee and migrant health systems to broader system resilience and global health security

continuity.value: Health, migration, and development systems are treated as connected across movement and settlement contexts rather than as isolated emergency phases

observations.method: WHO report overview and stated implications for integrating refugee and migrant health into public-health, migration-governance, development, and UHC agendas.
observations.uncertainty: System-level framing does not measure continuity of care, health outcomes, or resilience in every setting; health security language can also prioritize state surveillance over migrant agency and privacy if safeguards are weak.
observations.subgroup: People moving across borders, displaced populations, host communities, health workers, public-health agencies, and institutions responsible for UHC and emergency preparedness.
observations.counterinterpretation: Inclusive health systems may improve population health, but political backlash, resource scarcity, unequal host-community investment, and legal precarity can limit trust and actual use.

leadership.value: Stronger leadership, sustained investment, and enhanced coordination are identified as necessary to promote refugee and migrant health

data_monitoring.value: Strengthened data and monitoring systems are recommended for implementation tracking and accountability

affected_voice.value: The report recommends greater inclusion of refugees and migrants in decision-making processes

observations.method: WHO report recommendations derived from global evidence, the 93-country survey, policy analysis, and country case studies.
observations.uncertainty: Participation language does not establish representation, decision power, safety, compensation, or feedback closure; data systems can also create privacy and status risks for people with insecure legal positions.
observations.subgroup: Refugees and migrants, representative organizations, local communities, health and migration authorities, data stewards, and civil-society partners.
observations.counterinterpretation: Inclusion can be consultative rather than authoritative, and monitoring can improve administrative visibility without reducing discrimination, exclusion, or unequal bargaining power.

related_sources.claim: WHO publication page links the 122-page global report download.

boundary: This record adds a global refugee- and migrant-health signal on implementation monitoring, cross-sector integration, health equity, system resilience, data, participation, and governance. It is based on the WHO public report summary and its 93-country survey frame, not respondent-level microdata, a complete health-outcome evaluation, proof of equal access, or evidence that national roadmaps are implemented effectively.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official WHO publication page reviewed for report date, first global baseline claim, six priority areas, 93-country Global Survey on Health and Migration, six-region evidence base, integration agenda, recommendations, and report metadata.
